  You are revising ADR-0011 at D:/the-synaptic-sea-2d/docs/architecture/adr-0011-life-support-graph-data-model.md (project D:/the-synaptic-sea-2d, Godot 4.7.2 GDScript) after per-ADR engine and TD-ADR reviews and a cross-ADR adjudication of the Core tier.   ADR-0011 review verdict CONCERNS (non-blocking). No wrong API, no compile failure and no 4.7 incompatibility found. Packed-array, typed-return, reflection and var_to_bytes claims were all reproduced on 4.7.2 headless (editor binary, not a release export). Seven small amendments are recommended and two cross-ADR mismatches need an owner.:
  E1 [medium] A script error is not a Graph fault, and it aborts the function half-way. Probed on 4.7.2 headless: an out-of-bounds packed-array read logs `SCRIPT ERROR: Out of bounds get index` and the call returns 0. An out-of-bounds write logs `Out of bounds set index` and aborts the rest of the calling function, so the code after it never runs. In a release export this is a log line and a silently half-applied multi-column mutator. It will not raise `GraphFaults.*`, and `assert` is banned. The ADR's 'a stale id is harmless' rule (4.1 item 5) and the restore order (7.2 steps 3 and 8) are the only protection. Nothing in the ADR states that every index must be validated before the first write of a mutator.
    amendment: Add to 4.1 and the Implementation Guidelines: 'every mutator and phase validates all slots and indices before its first column write. An out-of-bounds packed-array access is a SCRIPT ERROR that aborts the function with no fault and no rollback in release. CI treats any SCRIPT ERROR log line as a failure (ADR-0010 load_all gate) and the fuzz corpus runs with the log scanned.' Add a Validation Criteria line: 'no SCRIPT ERROR in the log across the restore fuzz and the stale-id mutator tests.'
  E2 [medium] Reflection cannot see `static var`, and a static would be shared by every instance. Probe: `GraphState` with `static var _sv` is absent from `get_property_list()` filtered by `PROPERTY_USAGE_SCRIPT_VARIABLE`. The 6.3 reflection test would therefore never notice a persisted-looking static. The fresh scratch `GraphState` that `restore` builds would also share it with the live object, which breaks the two-phase restore.
    amendment: Add to 6.3 and the guidelines: 'GraphState, GraphCaches, GraphScratch and GraphDiag declare no `static var` (reflection does not list them and they are shared by every instance, including the restore scratch object). Constants and static funcs only.' Add this to the OWN-01 lexical rule, or to a one-line lint in the reflection test: scan the four files for `^static var`.
  E3 [low] RefCounted reference cycles leak. Probe: two RefCounted objects referencing each other produce `WARNING: ObjectDB instances were leaked at exit`. `GraphState` holds `_caches`, `_scratch` and `_diag` strongly, so any back-reference to `GraphState` from those three, or from `GraphView`, creates a cycle. The Key Interfaces snippet `_state._caches` shows the direction state to caches. ADR-0012 passes `GraphState` as a parameter, which is the safe form. The ADR states no rule, and 'reference cycles invite leaks' appears only in Alternative 1.
    amendment: Add a guideline: 'GraphCaches, GraphScratch, GraphDiag and GraphView hold no field of type GraphState. Ownership is one-way (GraphModule to GraphState to the three holders), and the writers receive the state as a parameter. Test: construct and free a full GraphModule in a headless test and assert no leak warning.'
  E4 [low] The aliasing rule in 6.2 (2) gives the wrong reason. It says `resize` would orphan an alias. Probe: `a = PackedInt32Array([1,2])`, `al = a`, `a.resize(5)` gives `al.size() == 5`. A `Packed*Array` Variant shares one ref, and resize happens in place. Only whole-member re-assignment (the Jacobi swap, restore phase 2) leaves an old alias pointing at the previous buffer. Probe: `duplicate()` isolates, so `snap[0]` stays 1 after `a[0] = 99`. The same probe confirmed that a payload column that is not duplicated sees later live writes. The rule is safe but over-restrictive and the stated cause is wrong. ADR-0012 has also replaced the `next`-swap in 6.2 (4) with accumulators.
    amendment: Reword 6.2 (2): 'a local alias is invalidated only by re-assigning the member (swap, restore phase 2); resize and element writes are visible through every alias.' Mark 6.2 (4) as superseded by ADR-0012 (accumulator apply). Rename the GraphScratch description 'Jacobi next columns' to 'Jacobi accumulators and flux arrays' in 1 and 6.1. In 7.2, state that the scratch GraphState is dropped immediately after phase 2, because the live members then share its buffers.
  E5 [low] Key Interfaces snippets are not valid GDScript as written, although the ADR says they follow ADR-0010 typing. The `GraphSchema` static funcs (`table_names`, `column_names`, `elem_type`, ...) have no trailing colon and no body. Several other lines carry a trailing `#` comment on the signature line. `GraphFault.raise_ctx` mutates the caller-owned `detail` Dictionary by reference (`detail["subject"] = subject`), so a shared or const-derived Dictionary would be mutated. Everything else compiled under the ADR-0010 warning regime (all warnings at error) in my probe project: `@abstract class_name` on one line, `const NAMES: Array[StringName]`, `const NOT_IN_SCOPE: int = (DOMAIN_ID << 16) | 1`, the `set_valve` flag expression, a mutually referencing GraphState and GraphCaches pair, and `GraphIds` constants named `OK` and `FAILED`.
    amendment: Label the GraphSchema block 'signatures only (bodies elided)', or give each func a `:` and `pass`. In `raise_ctx`, document 'detail is caller-owned and is written to' or copy it first. Keep the LINT-SPIKE-1 load-check caveat.
  E6 [low] `RoomSource` override hazards are real, and the ADR states only the first half. On 4.7.2 an override that omits `-> int` and returns on one path only fails with `Not all code paths return a value`. With ADR-0010's warning config it also fails with `has no static return type`. An override that misses the second abstract method fails with `Class ... must implement RoomSource.room_exposed_tiles() and other inherited abstract methods`. The ADR's 'tests inject a fake' does not say how. ADR-0010 3.5 requires hand-written `extends RoomSource` doubles, because gdUnit4 `mock()` of an `@abstract` class is unverified.
    amendment: In 11 (RoomSource) add: 'every override writes the explicit `-> int` and returns on all paths; fakes are hand-written `extends RoomSource` classes in tests/support (ADR-0010 3.5), not gdUnit4 mock().'
  E7 [low] The Engine Compatibility Knowledge Risk is MEDIUM, but VERSION.md rates 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 as HIGH, and ADR-0010 rates its own domain HIGH. This ADR depends on two 4.7 rows (typed-return override, packed element writes), `@abstract` (4.5) and typed Dictionary (4.4).
    amendment: Raise Knowledge Risk to HIGH, or state why the Core data-layout domain is lower than ADR-0010's.
  E8 [info] Plausibility of the 'probed' claims. I re-ran them on Godot 4.7.2 mono headless, which is the editor binary, so the release-export caveat stands. All reproduced. (a) mini/maxi/clampi/absi/signi return int. (b) `get_property_list()` filtered by `PROPERTY_USAGE_SCRIPT_VARIABLE` lists underscore members in declaration order and omits constants, enums and statics. (c) member swap by reference and the alias-sees-write behaviour hold. (d) `arr[i] = v` and `arr[i] += 2` on a packed member called a property setter 0 times, while whole-array assignment called it once. The ADR's own probe scripts (0011/p1..p3) never declare a setter, so (d) rests on ADR-0005 P8 and is confirmed here. (e) dup plus first write on 8192 int32 measured 0.744 us here against the ADR's 0.71, and `duplicate()` isolates. (f) typed `Dictionary[int,int].get(k,-1)` works. (g) int32 wrap of 3000000000 reads -1294967296, byte 300 reads 44, byte -1 reads 255. (h) a StringName key round-trips as type 21 and a String key as type 4. (i) the payload sizes reproduce exactly: 29,674 canonical / 29,560 var_to_bytes at 105/150/270, and 33,144 / 32,968 at 120/172/300. The fixture is synthetic: it assumes 60 `defs.off` entries and 1,500 `defs.utf8` bytes, which are not stated in the ADR.
    amendment: State the defs assumption (60 offsets, 1,500 utf8 bytes) next to claim (i) and the 3.11 size figure, so the 114-node reach-point is reproducible. Keep S0-a, S0-b and S3 on template_release.
  E9 [info] No deprecated or post-cutoff API misuse found. `duplicate()` is used on packed arrays only, so the 4.5 `duplicate_deep` note does not apply. `StringName` stays out of payloads. No Vector2i, float, `/`, `%` or untyped min/max appear in the snippets. `@abstract` is placed legally on the same line as `class_name`. A const typed array of StringName compiles. `SHADOWED_GLOBAL_IDENTIFIER` at error did not flag enum or const members named `OK` or `FAILED` inside `GraphIds`, but did flag member or param names `abs`, `hash`, `max`, `min`, `seed`, `tr`. No member or parameter named in the ADR collides with those, and no Object method name is used (`get`, `set`, `free`, `call`, `tr`, `connect` and `to_string` are absent from the accessor list). Unqualified use of `FAILED` outside `GraphIds` still resolves to the global Error constant, so callers must write `GraphIds.FAILED`.
    amendment: Add a one-line note in 4.7: 'always reference these as GraphIds.<NAME>; the unqualified OK and FAILED are @GlobalScope Error constants'.
  
  ADR-0011 review verdict CONCERNS:
  T1 [high, BLOCKING] Contradiction with ADR-0012 § 11 (and ADR-0017 D14.4) on the persisted/derived split. ADR-0011 § 6.1, § 7.4 (3) and Alternative 7 class `served_pm` as DERIVED and reject persisting it on read-cost grounds. ADR-0012 § 11 shows that a restore landing between the power hook (6n+0) and the atmo or failure hook (6n+2, 6n+4) cannot rebuild `served`, `draw` or the cable net load from the post-phase state: batteries have been debited, the thermostat duty has moved, a cable may have failed, or M10 has changed `req`. The restored run would then diverge in `hp` by one step's damage. Alternative 7 never addresses this restore-equivalence argument. As written, the control manifest would extract 'never persist served_pm', which is the opposite of what ADR-0012 phase 2 writes and ADR-0012's Implementation Guidelines require ('must never read served_pm from a cache').
    amendment: Adopt ADR-0012's request. (a) In § 3.2, add node columns `n_served` (i32 permille) and `n_draw` (i32, dJ per step), with canonical zero on every node that is not a power consumer and range specs in `GraphSchema`. (b) In § 3.4, define `e0` of a CABLE edge as its net load in W, with a stated sign convention and min/max. (c) In § 6.1, move `served_pm` from DERIVED to PERSISTED and add a row 'hook products: n_served, n_draw, CABLE e0, written by phase 2 only'. (d) Rewrite § 7.4 (3) to say post_restore re-derives `P`, `p_o2`, `o2_pm` and trend but never `served`. (e) Rewrite Alternative 7 so it rejects persisting only the intensive atmosphere values and cites ADR-0012 § 11 for the hook products. (f) Update § 3.11, Risks 1, the performance_budgets registry candidate and the Validation size line to about 30.5 KB with about 4.6 percent headroom. (g) Remove `served_pm` from the `derived_members.json` description. (h) Add GDD sync items for LS-21, LS-4 and TR-lsg-004 wording. If you refuse, say so explicitly and list ADR-0012's three boundary divergences (battery final step, thermostat flip, cable failure between hooks) as accepted known divergences.
  T2 [high, BLOCKING] `hdr.last_step_no` semantics conflict. § 2.3 defines it as 'the last step whose power hook completed' and says the step and `last_step_no` 'differ only between a tick and its first hook'. ADR-0012 § 1 (citing GDD LS-8) defines it as the last complete step, written by the failure hook at its end. ADR-0017's FAULT_GLOW reconcile (D6.4, 'reconcile only when GraphView.last_step_no() != hdr.fault_step_seen') and Failure & Trail's FT-15 poll depend on the failure-hook meaning: under ADR-0011's wording they would reconcile against a descriptor store that phase 11 has not yet rebuilt.
    amendment: Rewrite the last sentence of § 2.3: '`hdr.last_step_no` is the last step whose failure hook (phase 11) completed (LS-8, ADR-0012 § 1); it trails `step_no()` by up to one step, and equals it only from the end of the failure hook until the next power-hook tick.' Make § 3.8's hdr list and the `GraphView.last_step_no()` doc comment say the same.
  T3 [high, BLOCKING] The writer-file sets in § 1 (table), § 12.1, Implementation Guidelines and the registry candidate `graph_field_write_outside_writer_files` conflict with ADR-0012's design, so the proposed OWN-01 configuration would flag the code ADR-0012 specifies. (1) ADR-0012 puts the phases in a `src/sim/graph/propagate/` directory (twelve phase files plus a dispatcher), not the single file `graph_propagate.gd`. (2) `GraphCaches` is said to be written by `graph_derived.gd` only, but in ADR-0012: phase 7 writes the `P`, `p_o2`, `o2_pm` and trend caches; phase 11 writes the descriptor store and `caches.alarm_sections`; and every marker, including mutators in `graph_mutators.gd`, updates the last-emitted buckets ('updated at every mark, whoever marked it'). (3) `GraphScratch` is said to be written by the propagate file only, yet ADR-0012 sizes it through `GraphCaches.size_scratch()` from structural mutators and `post_restore`, and a `resize` is a mutating call under § 12.1.
    amendment: Rewrite § 12.1 and the § 1 table as one writer matrix per class. GraphState: `propagate/**`, `graph_mutators.gd`, `graph_restore.gd`. GraphCaches: `graph_derived.gd` plus either (i) `propagate/**` and `graph_mutators.gd` for the named members (intensive values, descriptor store, alarm list, last-emitted buckets), or (ii) a rule that phases and mutators write those members only by calling `GraphDerived` functions. State which option you choose. GraphScratch: `propagate/**` for contents, `graph_derived.gd` for sizing. Update the `field_writers.json` schema in Foundation Ask 1 to accept directory globs (merging ADR-0012 Foundation Ask 1), and update the forbidden_patterns registry candidate and the Implementation Guidelines to match.
  T4 [high, BLOCKING] The Graph side of ADR-0013's `LayoutGraphPort` is missing. ADR-0013 § 8 declares five abstract methods that 'the Graph's facade' implements: `check_instantiate(views, template_id: String) -> StringName`, `instantiate_section(scope, section_id, template_id, kind, out: SectionBases) -> int`, `opening_into(edge_id, out: OpeningRead) -> bool`, `seam_openings_into(seam_id, out: SeamOpenings) -> bool` and `section_counts_into(section_id, out: SectionCounts) -> bool`. ADR-0013 R7 says its §§ 3, 8 and 10 change if ADR-0011 does not supply them. ADR-0011 names none of the four reads and calls M1's out object `InstantiateResult`, where ADR-0013 calls it `SectionBases`. ADR-0011 § 1 and the ADR-0012 assumption also say Web Map's `init_world` calls M1 directly, but ADR-0013 routes it as Web Map → LM1 → port.instantiate_section, so that Layout allocates `section_id` first. A Layout or Graph story written today would pick one of two incompatible call chains.
    amendment: Add a § 9.5 'Layout port' and a Key Interfaces snippet. It should declare the Graph facade class (for example `GraphLayoutPort extends LayoutGraphPort` in `src/sim/graph/ports/`, injected by the composition root), implementing all five methods: allocation-free, caller-owned outs, valid in P3 and in P2 after the Graph's own writes. `opening_into` derives `door_state` from `area`. `seam_openings_into` returns `opening_ids` in `socket_plan.openings` order and stays valid after restore. `section_counts_into` reads persisted columns only (Tier S). `check_instantiate` is the pure CAPACITY and LS-18 reason check that ADR-0012 calls `check_instantiate_section`. Unify the out type name (one of `InstantiateResult` or `SectionBases`) in § 11 and the registry candidate. Reword § 1's 'init_world, binding_source' row and § 4.4: M1's only caller is Layout LM1 through the port, and LM1's only caller is Web Map `init_world` in the INIT scope.
  T5 [medium] A restore check for the hook cursors is missing and is now owned by nobody. ADR-0012 § 1 adds the runtime guard `HOOK_CURSOR` (local code 25) and asks ADR-0016 to verify `last_step_power/atmo/failure` against the restored clock. ADR-0016 has no cursor verifier (grep finds none), and its V3 row only cites ADR-0011 § 7.2's twelve steps. § 7.2's static [min, max] specs cannot classify a save whose `last_step_X` exceeds the step implied by `T`. Such a save restores successfully, and the first hook then raises HOOK_CURSOR mid-play, which turns a classifiable corrupt input into an in-play FAULTED.
    amendment: In one append-only batch, append local code 25 `HOOK_CURSOR` (ADR-0012's runtime guard) and code 26 `RESTORE_CURSOR` to § 8.1, then add a § 7.2 step after step 7. The step checks each `last_step_X` against the installed clock (ADR-0016 R2 installs it before R3): it must equal the step of the last tick at or before T on which hook X was due, under ADR-0012's step-0 convention, and `last_step_no == last_step_failure`. The reason is `RESTORE_CURSOR(hook, expected, got)`. Update the 1,000-mutation fuzz reason table, and record in Related that ADR-0016 V3 now covers it via § 7.2.
  T6 [medium] Stale-id reads are underspecified. § 4.1 (5) says a read of a stale or tombstoned id 'returns the neutral value', but defines it per getter nowhere. ADR-0017 assumes 'a not-live sentinel without faulting'. For `node_state(id)` the natural neutral 0 is `NODE_STATE` OK, the opposite of not-live: an Emitter or Interaction reader would treat a tombstoned or never-allocated node as healthy. The same ambiguity affects `edge_state`, `section_of` (0 is EXTERIOR's section) and `compartment_*`.
    amendment: Add a sentinel column to the § 9.1 hot-path list. Suggested values: `node_state`/`edge_state` return -1 (NOT_LIVE, outside the `NODE_STATE` domain); `node_kind` -1; `section_of` -1; `served_pm`/`run_pm`/`stock_pm`/`node_hp` 0; `compartment_*` -1 for a cid with no `comps` row. Alternatively, add `node_live(id)`/`edge_live(id) -> bool` and require readers to guard with it. Add a test that every hot getter answers its documented sentinel for id -1, an id at or above the counter, and a tombstone.
  T7 [medium] The purity statement in § 9.1 contradicts itself and ADR-0012 § 4. It says no getter 'writes any member of any of the four classes', then says the view 'may call `ensure_derived()`'. In ADR-0012 that call rebuilds `GraphCaches` and increments `GraphDiag.late_rebuilds` when it finds `topo_dirty` set. The property actually guaranteed is 'writes no persisted column, emits no key, draws no RNG; the hash is unchanged'.
    amendment: Reword § 9.1 purity: 'No getter writes any GraphState column, marks a dirty key or draws RNG, so `state_hash` is unchanged. The one permitted side effect is the defect-only `ensure_derived()` guard (ADR-0012 § 4), which writes GraphCaches and increments `GraphDiag.late_rebuilds`, asserted zero in every test.' Align the Implementation Guidelines bullet 'no write to any member'.
  T8 [medium] The snapshot-size evidence covers the at-weld roster only. The 29.7 KB fixture (about 30.5 KB after T1, 4.6 percent headroom) is the loaded set at the weld. Rows are never removed: tombstones persist in the payload, RAGGED cuts append stub HULL_SEGMENT rows, cut seams keep their lists, and `defs` never shrinks. ADR-0013 § 6 permits one weld-then-cut cycle per socket. The lifetime-worst reachable state (every socket cycled once with RAGGED cuts, every queue at its bound, all defs interned) is therefore larger than the measured fixture, and no Validation item measures it. Separately, § 3.11's '32 KB is reached near 114 nodes' is at most 9 nodes away.
    amendment: Add a 'lifetime-worst' fixture to Validation and § 3.11: every socket welded and cut RAGGED once (ADR-0013 § 6 bound), queues at bound, maximal defs. Either show it fits under 32 KB or pre-commit lever 1 (the fluid-stamp side table) now, with the tradeoff stated. Cite ADR-0013's one-cycle-per-socket rule as the bound that makes tombstone growth finite at MVP.
  T9 [medium] `GraphView`, the contract eight consumers code against, exists only as a prose list in § 9.1, with no Key Interfaces skeleton. Some reads that consumers need are absent from that list: a LOAD subtype getter for ADR-0028's fixture filter (TR-light-034 requires excluding non-Graph or self-powered fixtures and identifying lamp LOADs), a per-section compartment enumeration (TR-light-034's mean is per section, so a consumer must currently scan all compartments through `cid_at` and filter by `section_of`), and the descriptor-row getters of § 9.4, named only with ellipses.
    amendment: Add a `graph_view.gd` Key Interfaces skeleton with typed signatures and sentinel doc comments (T6) for every hot getter, including `load_subtype(id) -> int`, `compartments_in_section(section_id, out: PackedInt32Array) -> int` (ascending) and the full `desc_*` getter list. Tag each `## @hot` for the HOT-01 list.
  T10 [low] § 9.3 claims the descriptor store is sorted by construction, but the claim rests on unstated preconditions. The key is `(subject_kind << 40) | (subject_id << 8) | mode`, and the visit order is NODE, EDGE, COMPARTMENT, SEAM, OPENING. Strict ascent therefore requires the `GraphIds.SUBJECT_KIND` ordinals to be NODE < EDGE < COMPARTMENT < SEAM < OPENING, which is never pinned, and `ids.lock.json` would freeze whatever is written first. It also requires that OPENING edges are excluded from the EDGE pass, or that both passes cannot produce the same key, which is also unstated. The OPENING subject's anchor is undefined (the anchor bullet covers NODE, EDGE, COMPARTMENT and SEAM only).
    amendment: In § 4.7 or § 9.3, fix `SUBJECT_KIND` ordinals to the visit order (for example NODE 1, EDGE 2, COMPARTMENT 3, SEAM 4, OPENING 5). State that OPENING-kind edges are visited only in the OPENING pass. Define the OPENING anchor (for example `anchor_a` = edge id, `anchor_b` = -1).
  T11 [low] The Key Interfaces and internal text have drifted from each other and from ADR-0012. (a) The header's in-memory form is ambiguous: § 3.8 and the Implementation Guidelines say GraphState holds 'a Dictionary of int', while Key Interfaces declares `_h_*: int` members. The § 6.3 reflection allowlist differs between the two. (b) The `set_valve` snippet marks only EDGE and does not rebuild, but ADR-0012 § 6 says M8 changes connectivity, rebuilds and marks TOPO. Implementers copy snippets. (c) `GraphModule.setup` lacks ADR-0012's `work: WorkCounter`, the `graph.fail` stream registration and the ClockView source. (d) § 1 hard-codes 'divisor 6, offsets 0, 2, 4', where ADR-0012 makes both `GraphTuning` data. (e) `GraphFault.raise_ctx` mutates the caller's `detail` Dictionary.
    amendment: (a) Choose `_h_*` int members and state that the snapshot builds the hdr Dictionary. (b) Make the `set_valve` excerpt set `topo_dirty`, call `GraphDerived.ensure_derived`, and mark `EDGE` and `TOPO`, or cut it to a mutator that does not change connectivity (for example M10). (c) Adopt ADR-0012's `setup` signature. (d) Say 'divisor `tuning.graph_step_ticks`, offsets `tuning.hook_offset_*`'. (e) Copy `detail` before adding `subject`, or document the ownership transfer.
  T12 [low] Sibling ADRs have closed several items that ADR-0011 still carries open, and the Graph-side additions they ask for have not been adopted. Open Question 2 is closed by ADR-0016 (phase 0). Open Question 3 is closed by ADR-0012 § 7 (the EXOGENOUS clear rule). Open Question 8 and Risk 7 are closed by ADR-0012 § 8.2 (2-bit kind, 18-bit id), so § 4.1 (4) and § 8.4's '2^20 RNG subject field' becomes 2^18. Not yet adopted: `ONSET_UNKEYED` in the M1 check; `GraphIds.ALARM_CAPABLE_MASK`; the `GraphTuning` hook offsets, `load_queue_max`, `w_min_steps` and burst fields; the `GraphCaches` members `active_*`, `store_slots`, `machine_slots`, `exchange_links`, the POWER island list and `alarm_sections`; the `GraphDiag` counters `late_rebuilds`, `queue_dropped` and `footprints_clamped`; and the note that `FailureFilter.loaded_only` is always satisfied because the store holds loaded sections only.
    amendment: Mark Open Questions 2, 3 and 8 and Risk 7 as resolved, with pointers to the closing ADRs. Change 2^20 to 2^18 in § 4.1 (4) and § 8.4. Add a short 'Adopted from ADR-0012' list covering the GraphIds, GraphTuning, GraphCaches and GraphDiag additions, and require that `derived_members.json` includes them. Document `loaded_only` as retained for type stability and always true.
  T13 [low] Three smaller gaps. (a) § 4.6 describes the EMPTY state but not the ADR-0016 § 3.3 mechanism: `default_state(ctx)` must `ctx.put` a snapshot-shaped payload that the Graph's own `restore` accepts, and KRN-RST-07 tests that path. (b) After a restore of a store above a lowered `stock_cap`, readers and M16 `withdraw_store` see over-cap stock, and `stock_pm` can exceed 1000, for up to `GRAPH_STEP_TICKS - 1` ticks until the phase-0 reconcile; for a dormant section the window lasts until the section loads. Neither window is stated. (c) `RESTORE_UNKNOWN_DEF` (step 11) does not mention resolution through the ADR-0007 alias path, which ADR-0016 assumes. ADR-0007 defers aliases to a pre-SHIPPED story.
    amendment: (a) Add to § 4.6: '`default_state` builds this state as a payload with `GraphSchema` keys, `ctx.put`s it, and the kernel applies it through `GraphRestore.restore` (ADR-0016 § 3.3); the payload passes all § 7.2 steps.' attachment.content:
- adopt: Brownfield audit — do existing artifacts actually work? Numbered migration plan. Unlike /project-stage-detect, checks compliance not existence.
- agents-sdk: Build, debug, or review Cloudflare Agents SDK applications using the agents package.
- architecture-decision: Create an ADR documenting a technical decision: context, alternatives considered, consequences.
- architecture-review: Traceability matrix mapping GDD requirements to ADRs. Finds gaps, cross-ADR conflicts, engine compatibility. PASS/CONCERNS/NOT ASSESSED/FAIL.
- art-bible: Author the Art Bible — visual identity gating asset production. Run before /map-systems.
- asset-audit: Audit assets against naming conventions, file size budgets, format standards. Finds orphaned assets, missing references.
- asset-spec: Per-asset visual specs plus AI generation prompts from GDDs and character profiles. After the art bible.
- balance-check: Find balance outliers, broken progressions, degenerate strategies, economy imbalances in formulas and data. 'Check game balance'.
- basin: Build and troubleshoot Cloudflare Basin analytics workflows with Basin Pipelines, Basin Catalog, and Basin SQL. Use for streaming data into R2 Iceberg tables, managing catalogs, or querying those tables; also use for requests using the former Data Platform, Pipelines, R2 Data Catalog, or R2 SQL names.
- brainstorm: Guided concept ideation using professional studio techniques, player psychology, creative exploration.
- brownfield: First-principles audit and improvement plan for an EXISTING codebase ("brownfield" project) — especially one the user can run and demo but can't confidently judge. Orchestrates parallel specialist subagents (architecture, product-intent, code, tests, security, performance, docs) that treat existing code as evidence rather than ground truth, keeps an assumptions register and escalates the risky ones, writes a consolidated improvement design doc with a dependency-ordered PR plan sized to the repo, runs a writer↔reviewer loop until no critical/major issues remain, and optionally (--execute) implements the plan as worktree-isolated, reviewed git branches. Use this skill whenever the user says /brownfield, asks to audit / health-check / assess / sanity-check / "second opinion" an existing repo or legacy app, asks "is this built correctly?", "what's wrong with this codebase?", "a contractor/AI built this and I'm not sure it's right", wants a prioritized improvement or remediation plan for code that already exists, or is inheriting a project and wants to know where the bodies are buried — even if they never use the word "brownfield". Not for greenfield design of new systems or for reviewing a single small diff/PR.
- bug-report: Structured bug report from a description, or analyze code for potential bugs. Reproduction steps, severity.
- bug-triage: Re-evaluate open bugs — priority vs severity, assign to sprints, surface systemic trends. Run when the count grows.
- ccgs-code-review: Architectural code review — coding standards, SOLID, testability, performance concerns.
- changelog: Auto-generate a changelog from git commits and sprint data. Internal and player-facing versions.
- cloudflare: Discover and choose Cloudflare products for apps, APIs, AI agents, storage, networking, and security. Use for architecture and product selection, including when the user describes a need without naming a Cloudflare product; then find the relevant skill or documentation.
- cloudflare-email-service: Implement or troubleshoot Cloudflare Email Sending and Email Routing integrations and their delivery configuration.
- cloudflare-one: Design, configure, troubleshoot, or review Cloudflare One Zero Trust and SASE deployments. Use cloudflare-one-migrations for migration planning from other vendors.
- cloudflare-one-migrations: Assess and plan migrations from existing VPN, SWG, or SASE platforms to Cloudflare One, including policy mapping, parity gaps, and rollout.
- code-review: Review a branch, PR, commit range, or working tree with separate Standards and Spec tasks through review_run. Use when the user asks for a code review or asks to review changes since a fixed point.
- consistency-check: Scan GDDs against the entity registry for cross-document conflicts. Grep-first approach targets conflicting sections, different stats.
- content-audit: Audit GDD content counts against what's implemented — planned vs built.
- create-architecture: Author the architecture blueprint before code is written. Validates decisions against the pinned engine, flags knowledge gaps.
- create-control-manifest: Flat must-do/never-do rules sheet per system and layer, extracted from Accepted ADRs. ADRs explain why; this is actionable.
- create-epics: Turn GDDs plus architecture into epics — one per architectural module, with untraced requirements. Then /create-stories [epic-slug].
- create-stories: Break one epic into implementable stories embedding TR-ID, ADR guidance, acceptance criteria. Reads the control manifest. After /create-epics.
- design-review: Reviews one design document for completeness, internal consistency, implementability, and design standards. Before handing to programmers.
- design-system: Section-by-section GDD authoring for one system — walks through each required section, cross-references dependencies.
- durable-objects: Build, debug, or review Cloudflare Durable Objects code for persistent state and coordination.
- estimate: Estimate task effort from complexity, dependencies, velocity, risk. Structured estimate with confidence levels.
- gate-check: Ready to advance between development phases? PASS/CONCERNS/NOT ASSESSED/FAIL with blockers and required artifacts. 'Can we move to production?'
- help: What should I do next? Use when stuck or you don't know what to do.
- k2: Build and troubleshoot Cloudflare K2 or K2 Streams durable logs. Use for stream setup, producing from Workers or HTTP, configuring retention and inputs, and consuming through subscriptions.
- launch-checklist: Launch readiness across every department: code, content, store, marketing, community, infrastructure, legal, go/no-go sign-offs.
- legion: Route legion <command> requests to the Legion CLI for Claude Code.
- localize: Localization pipeline — find hardcoded strings, extract string tables, cultural review, VO, RTL, enforce string freeze.
- map-systems: Decompose a concept into individual systems, map dependencies, prioritize design order, create the systems index.
- milestone-review: Milestone progress review — completeness, quality metrics, risk, go/no-go recommendation. At checkpoints or before a deadline.
- nextjs-on-cloudflare: Build, migrate, and deploy Next.js apps on Cloudflare Workers with vinext. Use when starting a Next.js project on Cloudflare, moving an existing app to Workers, choosing between vinext and OpenNext, or setting up vinext for Workers. For setup, migration, or deployment, install vinext's upstream skills with `npx skills add cloudflare/vinext` if missing, then read and follow the applicable skill and docs.
- onboard: Onboarding doc for a new contributor or agent — project state, conventions, priorities relevant to the specified role.
- orchestrate-omp: Coordinate OMP subagents on substantial work. Use when parallel discovery, specialist review, or clearly partitioned implementation will shorten or strengthen the result; skip trivial tasks.
- patch-notes: Player-facing patch notes from git history and changelogs. Translates developer language into player communication.
- perf-profile: Performance profiling — find bottlenecks, measure against budgets, produce ranked optimization recommendations.
- playtest-report: Structured playtest report template, or turn existing playtest notes into structured feedback.
- project-stage-detect: Analyze project state, detect stage, identify gaps, recommend next steps. 'Where are we in development?'
- propagate-design-change: A GDD changed — scan ADRs and the traceability index for now-stale architectural decisions. Impact report, guides resolution.
- prototype: Concept prototype before GDDs — throwaway HTML, Engine or Paper build, PROCEED/PIVOT/KILL/NOT ASSESSED. After /brainstorm and /setup-engine.
- pstack-omp: OMP adapter for poteto-mode. Maps canonical pstack roles and lifecycle protocols to current OMP task agents, batching, isolation, IRC follow-ups, and durable result resources.
- qa-plan: QA test plan for a sprint — classifies stories by Logic/Integration/Visual/UI, covers automated tests, manual cases, smoke scope.
- quick-design: Lightweight spec for small changes — tuning adjustments, minor mechanics. Embeds directly into stories; skips full GDD.
- regression-suite: Map test coverage to GDD critical paths, find fixed bugs lacking regression tests, flag drift from new features.
- release-checklist: Pre-release checklist — build verification, certification requirements, store metadata, launch readiness.
- research: Research a question with high-trust primary sources and save cited findings. Use when the user requests research, documentation facts, or API facts.
- retrospective: Sprint or milestone retrospective from completed work, velocity, blockers. Actionable insights for the next iteration.
- reverse-document: Generate missing design or architecture docs from existing implementation — works backwards from code and prototypes.
- review-all-gdds: Holistic cross-GDD review — contradictions between systems, dominant strategies, economic imbalance, cognitive overload, pillar drift.
- sandbox-migrate-to-next: Migrate Cloudflare Sandbox apps from stable @cloudflare/sandbox to @cloudflare/sandbox@next (SDK 1.0 preview). Use sandbox-next for apps already on the preview.
- sandbox-next: Build or maintain Cloudflare Sandbox apps on @cloudflare/sandbox@next (SDK 1.0 preview). Use sandbox-migrate-to-next when porting a stable app.
- sandbox-stable: Build or maintain Cloudflare Sandbox apps on the stable @cloudflare/sandbox package. Use sandbox-next for preview apps and sandbox-migrate-to-next for stable-to-preview migrations.
- scope-check: Scope creep check — current scope versus the original plan. Flags additions, quantifies bloat, recommends cuts. 'Any scope creep?'
- security-audit: Security audit — save tampering, cheat vectors, network exploits, data exposure, input validation. Before public or multiplayer release.
- settings: View or change project config — effective merged values, or set locally in project.local.yaml.
- setup-engine: Configure engine and version. Pins it in CLAUDE.md; WebSearch fills reference docs when the version is beyond LLM training data.
- skill-improve: Improve a skill via a test-fix-retest loop — static checks, targeted fixes, keep or revert on score change.
- skill-test: Validate skill files for structural compliance and behavioral correctness. Four modes: static linter, spec, category rubric, audit.
- smoke-check: Critical-path smoke gate before QA hand-off — runs the automated suite. A failed check means the build is not QA-ready.
- soak-test: Soak test protocol for extended play — what to observe and log for slow leaks, fatigue, late-appearing edge cases.
- sprint-plan: New or updated sprint plan from the current milestone, completed work, and available capacity.
- sprint-status: Fast, concise sprint snapshot — burndown and emerging risks for situational awareness. 'How is the sprint going?'
- start: First-time onboarding — asks where you are, then guides you to the right workflow.
- story-readiness: Is a story implementation-ready? Checks clear acceptance criteria, open questions, ADR refs. READY/NEEDS WORK/BLOCKED/NOT ASSESSED.
- team-audio: Orchestrate the audio team — audio-director, sound-designer, technical-artist, gameplay-programmer — direction through implementation.
- team-combat: Orchestrate the combat team — game-designer, gameplay-programmer, ai-programmer, technical-artist, sound-designer, qa-tester — design through implement and validate.
- team-level: Orchestrate the level team — level-designer, narrative-director, world-builder, art-director, systems-designer, qa-tester — for complete area creation.
- team-live-ops: Orchestrate the live-ops team — live-ops-designer, economy-designer, analytics-engineer, community-manager, writer — for a season or live event.
- team-narrative: Orchestrate the narrative team — narrative-director, writer, world-builder, level-designer — for story, world lore, narrative-driven levels.
- team-polish: Orchestrate the polish team — performance-analyst, technical-artist, sound-designer, qa-tester — to optimize and harden a feature or area.
- team-qa: Orchestrate the QA team through a full testing cycle — qa-lead strategy and test plan, qa-tester case writing, execution, sign-off.
- team-release: Orchestrate the release team — release-manager, qa-lead, devops-engineer, producer — to execute a release from candidate to deployment.
- team-ui: Orchestrate the UI team through the UX pipeline — authoring, visual design, implementation, review, polish. Uses /ux-design, /ux-review, studio templates.
- tech-debt: Track, categorize and prioritize technical debt across the codebase — scans for debt indicators, maintains a register.
- test-evidence-review: Quality review of test files and evidence — goes beyond existence, evaluates assertion coverage. ADEQUATE/INCOMPLETE/MISSING/NOT ASSESSED per story.
- test-flakiness: Find flaky tests from CI logs — aggregates pass rates, spots intermittent failures, recommends quarantine. After multiple runs.
- test-helpers: Generate engine-specific test helper libraries — assertion utilities, factory functions, mocks in the engine's test folder. Reduces boilerplate.

# Global instructions (all projects)

## Dynamic Workflows: model choice

- Always use Sonnet 5.5 (`model: 'sonnet'`) or Haiku (`model: 'haiku'`) for worker agents in Dynamic Workflows (the Workflow tool's `agent()` calls), to preserve token usage. Use Haiku for mechanical stages (logging, formatting, simple extraction) and Sonnet for the rest.
- Opus or Fable is acceptable only as an advisor where needed: a senior reviewer, judge or verdict seat, never for bulk work such as planners, writers, fixers or scanners.
- Set `model` explicitly on every worker `agent()` call; do not let workers inherit the session model.

# Claude Code Game Studios -- Game Studio Agent Architecture

Indie game development managed through 49 coordinated Claude Code subagents.
Each agent owns a specific domain, enforcing separation of concerns and quality.

## Technology Stack

- **Engine**: Godot 4.7.2
- **Language**: GDScript
- **Version Control**: Git with trunk-based development
- **Build System**: SCons (engine), Godot Export Templates
- **Asset Pipeline**: Godot Import System + custom resource pipeline

> **Note**: Engine-specialist agents exist for Godot, Unity, and Unreal with
> dedicated sub-specialists. Use the set matching your engine.

## Project Structure

@.claude/docs/directory-structure.md

## Engine Version Reference

@docs/engine-reference/godot/VERSION.md


## Technical Preferences

`project.yaml` at the repo root is the primary config store — engine, specialists,
naming, platform, performance, modes. Skills resolve it via `resolve_config`
(see `.claude/docs/config-resolution.md`).

`.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md` is the **legacy fallback**, read on demand
when a key is absent from `project.yaml`. It is not imported here: before
`/setup-engine` runs it is almost entirely `[TO BE CONFIGURED]` placeholders, and
after it runs `project.yaml` holds the real values.

## Coordination Rules

@.claude/docs/coordination-rules.md

## Collaboration Protocol

**User-driven collaboration, not autonomous execution.**
Every task follows: **Question -> Options -> Decision -> Draft -> Approval**

- Agents MUST ask "May I write this to [filepath]?" before using Write/Edit tools
  (exempt: `active.md` appends, agent memory, a subagent's new file at the path
  its orchestrating skill named; see `.claude/rules/agent-memory.md`)
- Agents MUST show drafts or summaries before requesting approval
- Multi-file changes require explicit approval for the full changeset
- No commits without user instruction
- A skipped or dismissed question is not an answer: act on nothing, re-ask in
  plain text and wait
- Started outside this file's folder? Warn first: hooks, deny rules and the
  ask-first mode load only when Claude Code starts here

See `docs/COLLABORATIVE-DESIGN-PRINCIPLE.md` for full protocol and examples.

> **First session?** If the project has no engine configured and no game concept,
> run `/start` to begin the guided onboarding flow.

## Coding Standards

@.claude/docs/coding-standards.md

## Context Management

Read `.claude/docs/context-management.md` on demand — it is a reference, not
session context. Two of its conventions are load-bearing and cited by name
elsewhere in the repo, so they are restated here rather than lost:

- **`production/session-state/active.md` is the session checkpoint.** The file is
  the memory, not the conversation. Read it first after any compaction, crash, or
  `/clear`.
- **Helpers in `.claude/scripts/` emit observations, never verdicts.** A script
  that scores or judges will eventually contradict a mode or override it cannot
  see. (Cited by `artifact-check.sh` and `adr-dep-graph.sh`.)

# Directory Structure

```text
/
├── CLAUDE.md                    # Master configuration
├── project.yaml                 # Machine-readable project config — engine, modes, stage (source of truth)
├── .claude/                     # Agent definitions, skills, hooks, rules, docs
├── <code root>/                 # Game source code — THE PATH IS ENGINE-SPECIFIC, see below
├── assets/                      # Game assets (art, audio, vfx, shaders, data)
├── design/                      # Game design documents (gdd, narrative, levels, balance)
├── docs/                        # Technical documentation (architecture, api, postmortems)
│   └── engine-reference/        # Curated engine API snapshots (version-pinned)
├── tests/                       # Game test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest)
├── tools/                       # Build and pipeline tools (ci, build, asset-pipeline)
├── prototypes/                  # Throwaway prototypes (outside the code root)
├── production/                  # Production management (sprints, milestones, releases)
│   ├── session-state/           # Ephemeral session state (active.md — gitignored)
│   └── session-logs/            # Session audit trail (gitignored)
└── studio-tests/                # QA for the skills/agents themselves — /skill-test, /skill-improve
```

## The code root is engine-specific

**Two of the three supported engines will not build a project whose code sits in
`src/`.** This is not a style preference — it is a hard constraint of the engine's
own toolchain:

| `engine.name` | Code root | Why it cannot be `src/` |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `src/` | No constraint — Godot loads from `res://` anywhere under the project root. |
| **Unity** | `Assets/` | Unity compiles **only** `Assets/` and `Packages/`. Code outside them is invisible to the compiler. |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/` | UnrealBuildTool discovers modules under `Source/`; content lives in `Content/`. A module elsewhere is not built. |

**Resolve the code root from `engine.name` before writing any source file.** A
path shown as `src/…` alone is a Godot example: read it as *"the code root"* and
substitute the row above. `src/` is the table's Godot row, not a universal path.

**Tests follow the same rule** — the same compilers decide what they see:

| `engine.name` | Test root | Anywhere else |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/` | — |
| **Unity** | `Assets/Tests/EditMode/`, `Assets/Tests/PlayMode/` | not compiled: "0 tests, Passed" |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/Private/Tests/` | not built: "No automation tests matched" |

Read `tests/unit/[system]/` (or `integration/`) anywhere as the test root plus `[System]/`.

# Godot Engine — Version Reference

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Engine Version** | Godot 4.7 |
| **Installed at pin time** | 4.7.2.stable.mono.official.ed1daf0bf (matches pin; probed 2026-10-25 at `C:/Users/dasbl/Documents/Godot/`). 4.6.2 standard is also installed, unused. |
| **Release Date** | June 2026 (latest patch: 4.7.2, August 2026) |
| **Project Pinned** | 2026-10-17 |
| **Last Docs Verified** | 2026-10-17 (release timeline and 4.7 changes); 2026-02-12 (4.4-4.6 content) |
| **LLM Knowledge Cutoff** | May 2025 |

## Knowledge Gap Warning

The LLM's training data likely covers Godot up to ~4.3. Versions 4.5, 4.6
and 4.7 were released after the cutoff and introduced significant changes that
the model does NOT know about; 4.4 came out shortly before it and may be thinly
covered. Always cross-reference this directory before suggesting Godot API calls.

## Installed-Version Gap Warning

The warning above is one-directional — it covers the **model** knowing less than
this pin. The reverse gap is real and `/setup-engine` §3 creates it deliberately
("pin the newer one and upgrade later"): this reference can sit **ahead of the
installed editor**, and an agent citing it correctly then emits APIs that do not
compile locally. **Check `Installed at pin time` above before trusting a
version-qualified claim** — `NOT DETERMINED` means the gap is unknown, not absent.

## Post-Cutoff Version Timeline

| Version | Release | Risk Level | Key Theme |
|---------|---------|------------|-----------|
| 4.5 | Sep 2025 | HIGH | Accessibility (AccessKit), variadic args, @abstract, shader baker, SMAA |
| 4.6 | Jan 2026 | HIGH | Jolt default, glow rework, D3D12 default on Windows, IK restored |
| 4.7 | Jun 2026 | HIGH | AreaLight3D, HDR output, Asset Store replaces the Asset Library, VirtualJoystick, Jolt soft-body and world-boundary changes, typed-return overrides |

## Before the Cutoff

4.4 (Mar 2025, Jolt option, FileAccess return types) predates the May 2025
cutoff; the Knowledge Gap Warning still applies to it.

Dates from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/releases, checked 2026-10-17:
4.4 Mar 3 2025, 4.5 Sep 15 2025, 4.6 Jan 26 2026, 4.7 Jun 18 2026, 4.7.2 Aug 18
2026. Migration guides and release notes: `breaking-changes.md` § Sources.

# Agent Coordination Rules

1. **Vertical Delegation**: Leadership agents delegate to department leads, who
   delegate to specialists. Never skip a tier for complex decisions.
2. **Horizontal Consultation**: Agents at the same tier may consult each other
   but must not make binding decisions outside their domain.
3. **Conflict Resolution**: When two agents disagree, escalate to the shared
   parent. If no shared parent, escalate to `creative-director` for design
   conflicts or `technical-director` for technical conflicts.
4. **Change Propagation**: When a design change affects multiple domains, the
   `producer` agent coordinates the propagation.
5. **No Unilateral Cross-Domain Changes**: An agent must never modify files
   outside its designated directories without explicit delegation.
6. **Read Design Docs by Section**: A brief names the sections an agent needs
   by heading. Find a heading in a GDD, ADR or the art bible with the Grep
   tool (`^#`, content mode) and Read that range with offset and limit; read a doc
   whole only when the task needs all of it, and say why. `validate-read.sh`
   refuses a whole-file read of a doc over 40 KB.
7. **Nothing Goes Upstream**: Never file, open or comment on an issue or pull
   request in an engine, plugin or vendor repository, even when asked. Write a
   draft (`/bug-report` drafts only) and the user submits it.

## Model Tier Assignment

Read `.claude/docs/model-tiers.md` on demand. It carries the tier table, the
per-skill assignments and the authoring rule.

**Key point:** whether a skill's `model:` is used
depends on how the skill starts. Typed as `/skill-name`: yes, except a `haiku`
pin in auto mode. Started by Claude through the Skill tool: no. Never tell a
user a `haiku` skill saves money; an `opus` skill typed in a Sonnet session
costs more. The agent-side `model:` is a different mechanism, and is applied.

## Subagents vs Agent Teams

This project uses two distinct multi-agent patterns:

### Subagents (current, always active)
Spawned via the `Agent` tool within a single Claude Code session. Used by all
`team-*` skills and orchestration skills. Subagents share the session's
permission context, run sequentially or in parallel within the session, and
return results to the parent.

**When to spawn in parallel**: If two subagents' inputs are independent (neither
needs the other's output to begin), spawn both `Agent` calls simultaneously
rather than waiting. Example: `/review-all-gdds` **Phase 2** (consistency) and
**Phase 3** (design theory) are independent — spawn both at the same time.
Phase 1 loads the GDDs and both depend on it, so it is the one phase here that
must NOT be parallelised.

### Agent Teams (experimental — opt-in)
Multiple independent Claude Code *sessions* coordinated via a shared task list.
Opt-in only — read `.claude/docs/agent-teams.md` on demand before proposing one.

## Parallel Task Protocol

When an orchestration skill spawns multiple independent agents:

1. Issue all independent `Agent` calls before waiting for any result
2. Collect all results before proceeding to dependent phases
3. If any agent is BLOCKED, surface it immediately — do not silently skip
4. Always produce a partial report if some agents complete and others block

# Coding Standards

- All game code must include doc comments on public APIs
- Architecture decisions are recorded as ADRs in `docs/architecture/`. **How many is
  set by `modes.workflow`** — all ADRs at `full`, *critical* ADRs only at `standard`,
  and none required at `minimal`, where the decision log and `design/game-brief.md`
  carry the rationale instead. See `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.
- Gameplay values must be data-driven (external config), never hardcoded
- All public methods must be unit-testable (dependency injection over singletons)
- Commits must reference the relevant design document or task ID
- **Commit messages**: Use Conventional Commits format — `feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`. Reference the story or task ID in the body (e.g., `Story: EPIC-001-S02`).
- **Verification-driven development**: Write tests first when adding gameplay systems.
  For UI changes, verify with screenshots. Compare expected output to actual output
  before marking work complete. Every implementation should have a way to prove it works.
- **A parse check is not a run.** Every story that changes something
  player-observable is launched and observed before it closes, and the
  observation is a retained screenshot in `production/qa/evidence/`. Procedure
  per engine: `.claude/docs/run-and-observe.md`. Not waived at
  `qa.level: minimal` — tests are, the look is not.

# Design Document Standards

- All design docs use Markdown
- Each mechanic has a dedicated document in `design/gdd/`
- **How many of the 8 sections are required depends on `modes.workflow`** —
  all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system defines numeric rules — rates,
  curves, thresholds, costs; the system's `Category` is a hint, not the test) at
  `standard`, and no
  GDD at all at `minimal`, where `design/game-brief.md` is the design record.
  See `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`. The 8 sections:
  1. **Overview** -- one-paragraph summary
  2. **Player Fantasy** -- intended feeling and experience
  3. **Detailed Rules** -- unambiguous mechanics
  4. **Formulas** -- all math defined with variables
  5. **Edge Cases** -- unusual situations handled
  6. **Dependencies** -- other systems listed
  7. **Tuning Knobs** -- configurable values identified
  8. **Acceptance Criteria** -- testable success conditions
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale

# Testing Standards

## Test Evidence by Story Type

All stories must have appropriate test evidence before they can be marked Done:

| Story Type | Required Evidence | Location | Default Gate Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Logic** (formulas, AI, state machines) | Automated unit test — must pass | `tests/unit/[system]/` | BLOCKING |
| **Integration** (multi-system) | Integration test OR documented playtest | `tests/integration/[system]/` | BLOCKING |
| **Visual/Feel** (animation, VFX, feel) | Retained screenshot + lead sign-off | `production/qa/evidence/` | BLOCKING |
| **UI** (menus, HUD, screens) | Retained screenshot of each screen touched | `production/qa/evidence/` | BLOCKING |
| **Config/Data** (balance tuning) | Smoke check pass | `production/qa/smoke-[date].md` | ADVISORY |

# Directory Structure

```text
/
├── CLAUDE.md                    # Master configuration
├── project.yaml                 # Machine-readable project config — engine, modes, stage (source of truth)
├── .claude/                     # Agent definitions, skills, hooks, rules, docs
├── <code root>/                 # Game source code — THE PATH IS ENGINE-SPECIFIC, see below
├── assets/                      # Game assets (art, audio, vfx, shaders, data)
├── design/                      # Game design documents (gdd, narrative, levels, balance)
├── docs/                        # Technical documentation (architecture, api, postmortems)
│   └── engine-reference/        # Curated engine API snapshots (version-pinned)
├── tests/                       # Game test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest)
├── tools/                       # Build and pipeline tools (ci, build, asset-pipeline)
├── prototypes/                  # Throwaway prototypes (outside the code root)
├── production/                  # Production management (sprints, milestones, releases)
│   ├── session-state/           # Ephemeral session state (active.md — gitignored)
│   └── session-logs/            # Session audit trail (gitignored)
└── studio-tests/                # QA for the skills/agents themselves — /skill-test, /skill-improve
```

## The code root is engine-specific

**Two of the three supported engines will not build a project whose code sits in
`src/`.** This is not a style preference — it is a hard constraint of the engine's
own toolchain:

| `engine.name` | Code root | Why it cannot be `src/` |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `src/` | No constraint — Godot loads from `res://` anywhere under the project root. |
| **Unity** | `Assets/` | Unity compiles **only** `Assets/` and `Packages/`. Code outside them is invisible to the compiler. |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/` | UnrealBuildTool discovers modules under `Source/`; content lives in `Content/`. A module elsewhere is not built. |

**Resolve the code root from `engine.name` before writing any source file.** A
path shown as `src/…` alone is a Godot example: read it as *"the code root"* and
substitute the row above. `src/` is the table's Godot row, not a universal path.

**Tests follow the same rule** — the same compilers decide what they see:

| `engine.name` | Test root | Anywhere else |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/` | — |
| **Unity** | `Assets/Tests/EditMode/`, `Assets/Tests/PlayMode/` | not compiled: "0 tests, Passed" |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/Private/Tests/` | not built: "No automation tests matched" |

Read `tests/unit/[system]/` (or `integration/`) anywhere as the test root plus `[System]/`.

# Agent Coordination Rules

1. **Vertical Delegation**: Leadership agents delegate to department leads, who
   delegate to specialists. Never skip a tier for complex decisions.
2. **Horizontal Consultation**: Agents at the same tier may consult each other
   but must not make binding decisions outside their domain.
3. **Conflict Resolution**: When two agents disagree, escalate to the shared
   parent. If no shared parent, escalate to `creative-director` for design
   conflicts or `technical-director` for technical conflicts.
4. **Change Propagation**: When a design change affects multiple domains, the
   `producer` agent coordinates the propagation.
5. **No Unilateral Cross-Domain Changes**: An agent must never modify files
   outside its designated directories without explicit delegation.
6. **Read Design Docs by Section**: A brief names the sections an agent needs
   by heading. Find a heading in a GDD, ADR or the art bible with the Grep
   tool (`^#`, content mode) and Read that range with offset and limit; read a doc
   whole only when the task needs all of it, and say why. `validate-read.sh`
   refuses a whole-file read of a doc over 40 KB.
7. **Nothing Goes Upstream**: Never file, open or comment on an issue or pull
   request in an engine, plugin or vendor repository, even when asked. Write a
   draft (`/bug-report` drafts only) and the user submits it.

## Model Tier Assignment

Read `.claude/docs/model-tiers.md` on demand. It carries the tier table, the
per-skill assignments and the authoring rule.

**Key point:** whether a skill's `model:` is used
depends on how the skill starts. Typed as `/skill-name`: yes, except a `haiku`
pin in auto mode. Started by Claude through the Skill tool: no. Never tell a
user a `haiku` skill saves money; an `opus` skill typed in a Sonnet session
costs more. The agent-side `model:` is a different mechanism, and is applied.

## Subagents vs Agent Teams

This project uses two distinct multi-agent patterns:

### Subagents (current, always active)
Spawned via the `Agent` tool within a single Claude Code session. Used by all
`team-*` skills and orchestration skills. Subagents share the session's
permission context, run sequentially or in parallel within the session, and
return results to the parent.

**When to spawn in parallel**: If two subagents' inputs are independent (neither
needs the other's output to begin), spawn both `Agent` calls simultaneously
rather than waiting. Example: `/review-all-gdds` **Phase 2** (consistency) and
**Phase 3** (design theory) are independent — spawn both at the same time.
Phase 1 loads the GDDs and both depend on it, so it is the one phase here that
must NOT be parallelised.

### Agent Teams (experimental — opt-in)
Multiple independent Claude Code *sessions* coordinated via a shared task list.
Opt-in only — read `.claude/docs/agent-teams.md` on demand before proposing one.

## Parallel Task Protocol

When an orchestration skill spawns multiple independent agents:

1. Issue all independent `Agent` calls before waiting for any result
2. Collect all results before proceeding to dependent phases
3. If any agent is BLOCKED, surface it immediately — do not silently skip
4. Always produce a partial report if some agents complete and others block

# Advisor Tool

You have access to an `advisor` tool backed by a stronger reviewer model. It takes NO parameters -- when you call advisor(), your entire conversation history is automatically forwarded. They see the task, every tool call you've made, every result you've seen.

Call advisor BEFORE substantive work -- before writing, before committing to an interpretation, before building on an assumption. If the task requires orientation first (finding files, fetching a source, seeing what's there), do that, then call advisor. Orientation is not substantive work. Writing, editing, and declaring an answer are.

Also call advisor:
- When you believe the task is complete. BEFORE this call, make your deliverable durable: write the file, save the result, commit the change. The advisor call takes time; if the session ends during it, a durable result persists and an unwritten one doesn't.
- When stuck -- errors recurring, approach not converging, results that don't fit.
- When considering a change of approach.

On tasks longer than a few steps, call advisor at least once before committing to an approach and once before declaring done. On short reactive tasks where the next action is dictated by tool output you just read, you don't need to keep calling -- the advisor adds most of its value on the first call, before the approach crystallizes.

Give the advice serious weight. If you follow a step and it fails empirically, or you have primary-source evidence that contradicts a specific claim (the file says X, the paper states Y), adapt. A passing self-test is not evidence the advice is wrong -- it's evidence your test doesn't check what the advice is checking.

If you've already retrieved data pointing one way and the advisor points another: don't silently switch. Surface the conflict in one more advisor call -- "I found X, you suggest Y, which constraint breaks the tie?" The advisor saw your evidence but may have underweighted it; a reconcile call is cheaper than committing to the wrong branch.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
